prompt: The shop's application in `snet-app` opens `stshopprod.blob.core.windows.net` and nobody has built any other road. How do its packets reach the account?
hint: Where does a platform service live?

choices.text: Directly, because the account is in the same subscription as the network
choices.why: Sharing a subscription puts nothing inside the network. The account lives on Microsoft's side.

choices.text: Nowhere: a subnet cannot reach a storage account until peered with it
choices.why: Peering joins two virtual networks; an account is not a network.

choices.text: Through a private endpoint Azure creates on first use
choices.why: Nothing is created for you; a private endpoint is a resource somebody declares.

choices.text: To its public endpoint, like any client on the internet
choices.why: Right. Without a service or private endpoint, the public road is the only one.

prompt: After a service endpoint for `Microsoft.Storage` is switched on in `snet-app`, which address does the application connect to?
hint: Which road keeps the account's public door?

choices.text: A private address from `snet-app`
choices.why: A service endpoint gives the account no address in your network; that is a private endpoint.
That is the private endpoint of the next section, a different road.

choices.text: The account's public address, reached over the backbone
choices.why: Right. What changes is that the traffic carries the subnet's identity.

choices.text: Azure's resolver, `168.63.129.16`, which relays it
choices.why: That address answers DNS; it does not carry storage traffic.

prompt: Code running in `snet-app` is compromised, and the subnet has a service endpoint for storage with no policy. What can the attacker's copy of the shop's data now reach that the shop did not intend?
hint: A service endpoint opens a road to a service, not to an account.

choices.text: Any storage account in the region, theirs included
choices.why: Right. Without a service endpoint policy, the road leads to every account of that service.

choices.text: Nothing: the account's firewall allows only `snet-app`
choices.why: That firewall protects the shop's account. The attacker writes to an account of their own.

choices.text: Only accounts in other tenants that approved the subnet
choices.why: Approval belongs to private endpoints. A service endpoint asks nobody.

choices.text: The office network, through the VPN
choices.why: The service endpoint concerns traffic to Azure services, not to the office.

prompt: Why would deploying `se.bicep` leave `snet-app` without its network security group?
hint: What does the file say about the subnet, and what does it leave out?

choices.text: Service endpoints and network security groups cannot coexist
choices.why: They coexist on any subnet. The problem is what this file mentions.

choices.text: The file redeclares the subnet without one
choices.why: Right. A declaration replaces what an earlier one said; declare a subnet once, beside its network.

choices.text: Bicep removes properties it cannot validate
choices.why: The compiler removes nothing; it compiled what the file says.

choices.text: `existing` deletes the network's other subnets
choices.why: `existing` only refers to the network. It changes nothing.

prompt: Which of these does a service endpoint NOT give you? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three limits are listed in the section.

choices.text: Access from a peered network
choices.why: Right. It works only for traffic starting in that subnet.

choices.text: A way to switch off the account's public endpoint
choices.why: Right. The service keeps answering on its public address.

choices.text: A firewall rule on the account naming the subnet
choices.why: That is exactly what it gives: `virtualNetworkRules`.

choices.text: Access from the office over a VPN
choices.why: Right. Traffic from the office did not start in the subnet.

choices.text: Traffic that carries the subnet's identity
choices.why: That is the point of it.

prompt: What is a private endpoint, physically?
hint: It takes an address from a subnet.

choices.text: A copy of the storage account placed in your region
choices.why: The data stays where it is; nothing is copied.

choices.text: A route that sends the account's public address through your firewall
choices.why: A route changes where packets go; a private endpoint gives the account an address of yours.

choices.text: A virtual machine that proxies requests to the account
choices.why: There is no machine to manage: it is an interface, run by Azure.

choices.text: A network interface in your subnet, standing for one service
choices.why: Right. Private Link connects that interface to the service on Microsoft's side.

prompt: The first private endpoint placed in `snet-pe`, `10.20.4.0/24`, receives `10.20.4.x`. What is x?
hint: Azure keeps the first four addresses of every subnet.

prompt: The shop wants a private road to both the blob and the file service of `stshopprod`. How many private endpoints does it need?
hint: Look at `groupIds`.

choices.text: One, since both services belong to one account
choices.why: An endpoint stands for one sub-resource of the account.

choices.text: Two, one per sub-resource
choices.why: Right. And each has its own zone: `privatelink.blob...` and `privatelink.file...`.

choices.text: One per subnet that wants to reach them
choices.why: One endpoint serves every network that can route to it and resolves its name.

choices.text: None: a service endpoint covers both
choices.why: A service endpoint is the other road, and it keeps the public door.

prompt: A partner creates a private endpoint to one of the shop's accounts from their own tenant. What state is the connection in until somebody at the shop acts?
hint: Who has permission on the account?

choices.text: *Pending*, waiting for the owner to approve it
choices.why: Right. Which is how a partner gets one private road and nothing else.

choices.text: Rejected, because cross-tenant endpoints are forbidden
choices.why: Cross-tenant endpoints are allowed; they wait for the owner.

choices.text: Approved, because private endpoints never need approval
choices.why: Approval is automatic only when the creator has permission on the resource.

choices.text: Disconnected, until the partner peers the two networks
choices.why: No peering is involved; Private Link connects the interface to the service.

prompt: Why does `pe.bicep` name its zone with `environment().suffixes.storage` instead of writing `core.windows.net`?
hint: What did the linter say about the hand-written version?

choices.text: Because a literal name fails to compile
choices.why: `hard.bicep` compiled; the linter warned.

choices.text: Because private zones may not contain dots
choices.why: The zone's name is full of dots either way.

choices.text: To keep working in sovereign clouds
choices.why: Right. Each cloud has its own storage suffix; `no-hardcoded-env-urls` guards it.

choices.text: Because Bicep charges less for expressions than for strings
choices.why: Nothing is charged for a template's contents.

prompt: Match each resource in `pe.bicep` to what it does.
hint: Five resources, and only two are the endpoint.

pairs.right: an interface in `snet-pe` for the blob service
writes the endpoint's address into the zone

right_distractors: gives the account a public address

prompt: The subnet property `privateEndpoint___Policies` makes filters and routes apply to private endpoints.
hint: Lessons 17 and 18 are about these.

prompt: What name does the application use after the private endpoint exists?
hint: The certificate carries one name.

choices.text: The same `stshopprod.blob.core.windows.net` as before
choices.why: Right. Only the answer to the name changes.

choices.text: `stshopprod.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net`, written into its settings
choices.why: That is the middle link of the chain; the certificate does not carry it.

choices.text: The address `10.20.4.4`, typed instead of a name
choices.why: Connecting by address would fail the certificate check.

choices.text: A new name Azure assigns to the endpoint
choices.why: No new name is given to the application to use.

prompt: Why is the shop's private zone called `privatelink.blob.core.windows.net` and not `blob.core.windows.net`?
hint: What would a zone called `blob.core.windows.net` answer for?

choices.text: Because Azure reserves `blob.core.windows.net` for the public DNS
choices.why: The reason is what the zone would answer for, not a reservation.

choices.text: So it answers only the middle link, leaving other accounts public
choices.why: Right. A `blob.core.windows.net` zone would break every account without an endpoint.

choices.text: Because a private zone's name must start with `privatelink`
choices.why: `shop.internal`, in lesson 21, is a private zone too.

choices.text: Because the certificate names the `privatelink` host
choices.why: The certificate names the account's ordinary host.

prompt: A developer on the office VPN runs `dig stshopprod.blob.core.windows.net` and gets a public address, while a VM in `vnet-shop-prod` gets `10.20.4.4`. What is missing?
hint: Who answered the laptop's question?

choices.text: A second private endpoint for the office
choices.why: One endpoint serves the office too, once its name resolves there.

choices.text: A service endpoint on the VPN gateway's subnet
choices.why: A service endpoint does not change any DNS answer.

choices.text: Nothing: the office is meant to use the public road
choices.why: With public access disabled, the public road leads to a refusal.

choices.text: A conditional forwarder from the office DNS into Azure
choices.why: Right. The laptop asks the office DNS, which asked the internet.

prompt: In the captured chain of `login.microsoftonline.com`, which link shows the Private Link pattern?
hint: Look for a zone name.

choices.text: The first, `login.mso.msidentity.com`
choices.why: That is an ordinary alias; nothing private can take it over.

choices.text: The last one, which changed between runs
choices.why: That link spreads sign-ins across places; lesson 22 is about it.

choices.text: `ak.privatelink.msidentity.com`, the second of the three
choices.why: Right. A network with a private zone of that name could answer it differently.

choices.text: None: Private Link does not appear in public DNS
choices.why: It does: the `privatelink` link is in the public chain on purpose.

prompt: Inside a virtual network, Azure's own resolver answers at the address `168.63.129.___`.
hint: The same address every network uses.

prompt: A VM in `vnet-shop-staging` resolves the account's name to its public address, though `vnet-shop-prod` gets `10.20.4.4`. Both use Azure's resolver. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Which networks does the zone answer?

choices.text: The account's public access was switched back on
choices.why: That changes whether the public address answers, not what the name resolves to.

choices.text: Staging subscriptions cannot use private endpoints
choices.why: Nothing about a subscription's name restricts the feature.

choices.text: The zone group wrote the wrong address
choices.why: Production gets the right one from the same zone.

choices.text: The zone has no link to `vnet-shop-staging`
choices.why: Right. A zone answers only the networks linked to it.

prompt: Put the steps of the private road in the order a request from `snet-app` takes them.
hint: The name is resolved before any packet is sent.
items: the packets go to the interface in `snet-pe`
Private Link carries them to the account's blob service
trap: Every failure in the section is a break between the second and third steps.

prompt: The shop disables public access on `stshopprod` before creating its private endpoint. What happens to the application in `snet-app`, which has a service endpoint?
hint: Which road ends at the public endpoint?

choices.text: Nothing, since the service endpoint bypasses the public endpoint
choices.why: It does not bypass it; it reaches it over the backbone.

choices.text: It loses access until the private endpoint exists
choices.why: Right. Roads 1 and 2 end at the public endpoint, and that is what was closed.

choices.text: It switches to the private road on its own
choices.why: There is no private road until the endpoint and its DNS exist.

choices.text: It keeps access, but only for reading
choices.why: Disabling public access does not distinguish reads from writes.

prompt: Which of these did the lab actually do in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at what has a transcript.

choices.text: Compiled a private endpoint, its zone, link and zone group
choices.why: Right. `az bicep build` on `pe.bicep`.

choices.text: Resolved a storage account's name to `10.20.4.4`
choices.why: That needs a real endpoint and a network inside Azure; it was taught, not run.

choices.text: Asked the public DNS for a Microsoft name's chain
choices.why: Right. `dig login.microsoftonline.com`.

choices.text: Ran Bicep's linter over a hand-written zone name
choices.why: Right. `no-hardcoded-env-urls`.

choices.text: Approved a pending private endpoint connection
choices.why: Approval is a request to Resource Manager; nothing was sent.
